Rotation lock and the locked rotation are system settings. To change them from the Quick Settings tile or a per-app rule, Android requires the "Modify system settings" permission.

Curmudgeon Rotation only writes two settings: auto-rotate on/off and the locked rotation. It remembers your previous values and puts them back when a rule ends.

On the next screen, switch on "Allow modifying system settings", then come back.

Some apps lock their own orientation (for example HBO Max stays portrait even with auto-rotate on). Changing system settings can't override that.

The "force" options add an invisible, zero-size window that asks Android for an orientation. It draws nothing and can't be touched.

That window can come from the accessibility service (no extra permission) or from "Display over other apps". Allow it on the next screen if you want to use app overlays or force rotation from the tile without the accessibility service.

Note: on Android 12 and newer, apps can hide app overlays while they are open, so forcing may not work in every app. The accessibility overlay is not affected by that.

To switch rotation when you open a specific app, Curmudgeon Rotation needs to know which app is in front. Android provides this through an accessibility service.

What it reads: only which app and screen is in front (the package name and the screen's class name, for example com.google.android.youtube).

What it does not read: window content, text you type or see, passwords, notifications or gestures.

What happens to it: it is used on your device to pick a rule. A short list of recently seen screens is kept in the app's private storage so you can limit rules to specific screens; you can view and clear it in settings. Nothing is transmitted. The app has no internet permission.

The same service can also hold the invisible overlay window used by the "force" rules.

On the next screen, find "Curmudgeon Rotation: per-app rules" under installed or downloaded apps and switch it on.

If the switch is greyed out ("Restricted setting"), Android is blocking it because the app was not installed from a store: open app info, tap the ⋮ menu, choose "Allow restricted settings", then try again.

An alternative to the accessibility service. With usage access, Curmudgeon Rotation checks which app was opened most recently, once per poll interval (default 1 second), only while the screen is on.

It reacts a little slower than the accessibility service and needs a small ongoing notification so Android keeps it running.

The usage data is read on your device only to pick a rule. Nothing is transmitted. The app has no internet permission.

On the next screen, choose Curmudgeon Rotation and switch on "Permit usage access".

One tap cycles: auto-rotate → locked portrait → locked landscape → auto-rotate off. Press and hold the tile to switch auto-rotate on or off.

Privacy: the app has no internet permission, so nothing can leave your device. The accessibility service only reads which app and screen is in front. Rules, settings and the recently-seen-screens log stay in the app's private storage, and are excluded from cloud backup. Exported rule files go only where you save them.
